entries.fee0c9c6829cb59e221bcb8e0c34b32958b0dbf9: <div sID="gen4339" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="Josh.11" sID="Josh.11"/> <div eID="gen4339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4340" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4341" type="x-p"/> This chapter continues and concludes the history of the conquest of Canaan; of the reduction of the southern parts we had an account in the foregoing chapter, after which we may suppose Joshua allowed his forces some breathing-time; now here we have the story of the war in the north, and the happy success of that war. I. The confederacy of the northern crowns against Israel, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.1-Josh.11.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. The encouragement which God gave to Joshua to engage them, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.6">ver. 6</reference>. III. His victory over them, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.7-Josh.11.9">ver. 7-9</reference>. IV. The taking of their cities, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.10-Josh.11.15">ver. 10-15</reference>. V. The destruction of the Anakim, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.21-Josh.11.22">ver. 21, 22</reference>. VI. The general conclusion of the story of this war, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.16-Josh.11.20">ver. 16-20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.23">23</reference>.
entries.8c8c8498ab3cf3e438340a96f47f501c2dd86f6f: <div eID="gen4341" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4340" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Confederacy Against Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1450.)</title> <div sID="gen4342" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass, when Jabin king of Hazor had heard <hi type="italic">those things,</hi> that he sent to Jobab king of Madon, and to the king of Shimron, and to the king of Achshaph, <hi type="super">2</hi> And to the kings that <hi type="italic">were</hi> on the north of the mountains, and of the plains south of Chinneroth, and in the valley, and in the borders of Dor on the west, <hi type="super">3</hi> <hi type="italic">And to</hi> the Canaanite on the east and on the west, and <hi type="italic">to</hi> the Amorite, and the Hittite, and the Perizzite, and the Jebusite in the mountains, and <hi type="italic">to</hi> the Hivite under Hermon in the land of Mizpeh. <hi type="super">4</hi> And they went out, they and all their hosts with them, much people, even as the sand that <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon the sea shore in multitude, with horses and chariots very many. <hi type="super">5</hi> And when all these kings were met together, they came and pitched together at the waters of Merom, to fight against Israel. <hi type="super">6</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Joshua, Be not afraid because of them: for to morrow about this time will I deliver them up all slain before Israel: thou shalt hough their horses, and burn their chariots with fire. <hi type="super">7</hi> So Joshua came, and all the people of war with him, against them by the waters of Merom suddenly; and they fell upon them. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> delivered them into the hand of Israel, who smote them, and chased them unto great Zidon, and unto Misrephoth-maim, and unto the valley of Mizpeh eastward; and they smote them, until they left them none remaining. <hi type="super">9</hi> And Joshua did unto them as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> bade him: he houghed their horses, and burnt their chariots with fire. <div eID="gen4342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4343" type="x-p"/> We are here entering upon the story of another campaign that Joshua made, and it was a glorious one, no less illustrious than the former in the success of it, though in respect of miracles it was inferior to it in glory. The wonders God then wrought for them were to animate and encourage them to act vigorously themselves. Thus the war carried on by the preaching of the gospel against Satan's kingdom was at first forwarded by miracles; but, the war being by them sufficiently proved to be of God, the managers of it are now left to the ordinary assistance of divine grace in the use of the sword of the Spirit, and must not expect hail-stones nor the standing still of the sun. In this story we have, <div eID="gen4343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4344" type="x-p"/> I. The Canaanites taking the field against Israel. They were the aggressors, God hardening their hearts to begin the war, that Israel might be justified beyond exception in destroying them. Joshua and all Israel had returned to the camp at Gilgal, and perhaps these kings knew no other than that they intended to sit down content with the conquest they had already made, and yet they prepare war against them. Note, Sinners bring ruin upon their own heads, so that <hi type="italic">God will be justified when he speaks,</hi> and they alone shall bear the blame for ever. Judah had now <hi type="italic">couched as a lion gone up from the prey;</hi> if the northern kings rouse him up, it is at their peril, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.9">Gen. xlix. 9</reference>. Now, 1. Several nations joined in this confederacy, some <hi type="italic">in the mountains</hi> and some <hi type="italic">in the plains,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.11.2">v. 2</reference>. Canaanites from east and west, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, &c. (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.3">v. 3</reference>), of different constitutions and divided interests among themselves, and yet they here unite against Israel as against a common enemy. Thus are <hi type="italic">the children of this world</hi> more unanimous, and therein <hi type="italic">wiser, than the children of light.</hi> The oneness of the church's enemies should shame the church's friends out of their discords and divisions, and engage them to be one. 2. The head of this confederacy was <hi type="italic">Jabin king of Hazor</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.1">v. 1</reference>), as Adoni-zedec was of the former; it is said (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.10">v. 10</reference>) Hazor had been the <hi type="italic">head of all those kingdoms,</hi> which could not have revolted without occasioning ill-will; but this was forgotten and laid aside upon this occasion, by consent of parties, <reference osisRef="Luke.23.12">Luke xxiii. 12</reference>. When they had all drawn up their forces together, every kingdom bringing in its quota, they were a very great army, much greater than the former, <hi type="italic">as the sand on the sea shore in multitude,</hi> and upon this account much stronger and more formidable, that they had horses and chariots very many, which we do not find the southern kings had; hereby they had a great advantage against Israel, for their army consisted only of foot, and they never brought horses nor chariots into the field. Josephus tells us that the army of the Canaanites consisted of 300,000 foot, 10,000 horses, and 20,000 chariots. <hi type="italic">Many there be that rise up</hi> against God's Israel; doubtless their numbers made them very confident of success, but it proved that so much the greater slaughter was made of them. <div eID="gen4344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4345" type="x-p"/> II. The encouragement God gave to Joshua to give them the meeting, even upon the ground of their own choosing (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Be not afraid because of them.</hi> Joshua was remarkable for his courage—it was his master grace, and yet it seems he had need to be again and again cautioned not to be afraid. Fresh dangers and difficulties make it necessary to fetch in fresh supports and comforts from the word of God, which we have always nigh unto us, to be made use of in every time of need. Those that have God on their side need not be disturbed at the number and power of their enemies; <hi type="italic">more are those that are with us than those that are against us;</hi> those have the hosts of the Lord that have the Lord of hosts engaged for them. For his encouragement, 1. God assures him of success, and fixes the hour: <hi type="italic">To-morrow about this time,</hi> when an engagement (it is probable) was expected and designed on both sides, <hi type="italic">I will deliver them up slain.</hi> Though they were to be slain by the sword of Israel, yet it is spoken of as God's work, that he would deliver them up. 2. He appoints him to <hi type="italic">hough their horses, hamstring</hi> them, <hi type="italic">lame</hi> them, and <hi type="italic">burn their chariots,</hi> not only that Israel might not use them hereafter, but that they might not fear them now, their God designing this contempt to be put upon them. Let Israel look upon their chariots but as rotten wood designed for the fire, and their horses of war as disabled things, scarcely good enough for the cart. This encouragement which God here gave to Joshua no doubt he communicated to the people, who perhaps were under some apprehensions of danger from this vast army, notwithstanding the experience they had had of God's power engaged for them. And the wisdom and goodness of God are to be observed, (1.) In infatuating the counsels of the enemy, that all the kings of Canaan, who were not dispersed at such a distance from each other but that they might have got all together in a body, did not at first confederate against Israel, but were divided in to the southern and northern combination, and so became the less formidable. And, (2.) In preparing his people to encounter the greater force, by breaking the less. They first engage with five kings together, and now with many more. God proportions our trials to our strength and our strength to our trials. <div eID="gen4345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4346" type="x-p"/> III. Joshua's march against these confederate forces, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.7">v. 7</reference>. He <hi type="italic">came upon them suddenly,</hi> and surprised them in their quarters. He made this haste, 1. That he might put them into the greater confusion, by giving them an alarm, when they little thought he was near them. 2. That he might be sure not to come short of the honour God had fixed, to give him the meeting at the enemies' camp, <hi type="italic">to-morrow about this time.</hi> It is fit we should keep time with God. <div eID="gen4346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4347" type="x-p"/> IV. His success, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.8">v. 8</reference>. He obtained the honour and advantage of a complete victory; he smote them and chased them, in the several ways they took in their flight; some fled towards Zidon, which lay to the northwest, others towards Mizpeh, eastward, but the parties Joshua sent out pursued them each way. So <hi type="italic">the Lord delivered them into the hand of Israel;</hi> they would not deliver themselves into the hands of Israel to be made proselytes and tributaries, and so offered up to God's grace (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.16">Rom. xv. 16</reference>), and therefore God delivered them into their hands to be made sacrifices to his justice; for God will be honoured by us or upon us. <div eID="gen4347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4348" type="x-p"/> V. His obedience to the orders given him, in destroying the horses and chariots (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.9">v. 9</reference>), which was an instance, 1. Of his subjection to the divine will, as one under authority, that must do as he is bidden. 2. Of his self-denial, and crossing his own genius and inclination in compliance with God's command. 3. Of his confidence in the power of God engaged for Israel, which enabled them to despise the chariots and horses which others trusted in, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Ps. xx. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.33.17">xxxiii. 17</reference>. 4. Of his care to keep up in the people the like confidence in God, by taking that from them which they would be tempted to trust too much to. This was <hi type="italic">cutting of a right hand.</hi>
entries.143d32e7696d79444734a7921cd2e93f9720593d: <div eID="gen4348" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Joshua's Victories. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1450.)</title> <div sID="gen4349" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And Joshua at that time turned back, and took Hazor, and smote the king thereof with the sword: for Hazor beforetime was the head of all those kingdoms. <hi type="super">11</hi> And they smote all the souls that <hi type="italic">were</hi> therein with the edge of the sword, utterly destroying <hi type="italic">them:</hi> there was not any left to breathe: and he burnt Hazor with fire. <hi type="super">12</hi> And all the cities of those kings, and all the kings of them, did Joshua take, and smote them with the edge of the sword, <hi type="italic">and</hi> he utterly destroyed them, as Moses the servant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded. <hi type="super">13</hi> But <hi type="italic">as for</hi> the cities that stood still in their strength, Israel burned none of them, save Hazor only; <hi type="italic">that</hi> did Joshua burn. <hi type="super">14</hi> And all the spoil of these cities, and the cattle, the children of Israel took for a prey unto themselves; but every man they smote with the edge of the sword, until they had destroyed them, neither left they any to breathe. <div eID="gen4349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4350" type="x-p"/> We have here the same improvement made of this victory as was made of that in the foregoing chapter. 1. The destruction of Hazor is particularly recorded, because in it, and by the king thereof, this daring design against Israel was laid, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.10-Josh.11.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. The king of Hazor, it seems, escaped with his life out of the battle, and thought himself safe when he had got back into his own city, and Joshua had gone in pursuit of the scattered troops another way. But it proved that that which he thought would be for his welfare was his trap; in it <hi type="italic">he was taken as in an evil net;</hi> there he was slain, and his city, for his sake, burned. Yet we find that the remains of it being not well looked after by Israel the Canaanites rebuilt it, and settled there under another king of the same name, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.2">Judg. iv. 2</reference>. 2. The rest of the cities of that part of the country are spoken of only in general, that Joshua got them all into his hands, but did not burn them as he did Hazor, for Israel was to dwell in <hi type="italic">great and goodly cities which they builded not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.6.10">Deut. vi. 10</reference>) and in these among the rest. And here we find Israel rolling in blood and treasure. (1.) In the blood of their enemies; <hi type="italic">they smote all the souls</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.1">v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">neither left they any to breathe</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.14">v. 14</reference>), that there might be none to infect them with the abominations of Canaan, and none to disturb them in the possession of it. The children were cut off, lest they should afterwards lay claim to any part of this land in the right of their parents. (2.) In the wealth of their enemies. The spoil, and the cattle, they <hi type="italic">took for a prey to themselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.11.14">v. 14</reference>. As they were enriched with the spoil of their oppressors when they came out of Egypt, wherewith to defray the charges of their apprenticeship in the wilderness, so they were now enriched with the spoil of their enemies for a stock wherewith to set up in the land of Canaan. Thus is the wealth of the sinner laid up for the just.
entries.bbfe4d27f4ffb1d27f72f54e2bcc70f26fce0c51: <div eID="gen4350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4351" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> As the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses his servant, so did Moses command Joshua, and so did Joshua; he left nothing undone of all that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses. <hi type="super">16</hi> So Joshua took all that land, the hills, and all the south country, and all the land of Goshen, and the valley, and the plain, and the mountain of Israel, and the valley of the same; <hi type="super">17</hi> <hi type="italic">Even</hi> from the mount Halak, that goeth up to Seir, even unto Baal-gad in the valley of Lebanon under mount Hermon: and all their kings he took, and smote them, and slew them. <hi type="super">18</hi> Joshua made war a long time with all those kings. <hi type="super">19</hi> There was not a city that made peace with the children of Israel, save the Hivites the inhabitants of Gibeon: all <hi type="italic">other</hi> they took in battle. <hi type="super">20</hi> For it was of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to harden their hearts, that they should come against Israel in battle, that he might destroy them utterly, <hi type="italic">and</hi> that they might have no favour, but that he might destroy them, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses. <hi type="super">21</hi> And at that time came Joshua, and cut off the Anakims from the mountains, from Hebron, from Debir, from Anab, and from all the mountains of Judah, and from all the mountains of Israel: Joshua destroyed them utterly with their cities. <hi type="super">22</hi> There was none of the Anakims left in the land of the children of Israel: only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod, there remained. <hi type="super">23</hi> So Joshua took the whole land, according to all that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses; and Joshua gave it for an inheritance unto Israel according to their divisions by their tribes. And the land rested from war. <div eID="gen4351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4352" type="x-p"/> We have here the conclusion of this whole matter. <div eID="gen4352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4353" type="x-p"/> I. A short account is here given of what was done in four things:—1. The obstinacy of the Canaanites in their opposition to the Israelites. It was strange that though it appeared so manifestly that God fought for Israel, and in every engagement the Canaanites had the worst of it, yet they stood it out to the last; not one city made peace with Israel, but the Gibeonites only, who understood the things that belonged to their peace better than their neighbours, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.19">v. 19</reference>. It is intimated that other cities might have made as good terms for themselves, without ragged clothes and clouted shoes, if they would have humbled themselves, but they never so much as <hi type="italic">desired conditions of peace.</hi> We here are told whence this unaccountable infatuation came: <hi type="italic">It was of the Lord to harden their hearts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.11.20">v. 20</reference>. As Pharaoh's heart was hardened by his own pride and wilfulness first, and afterwards by the righteous judgment of God, to his destruction, so were the hearts of these Canaanites. To punish them for all their other follies, God left them to this, to make those their enemies whom they might have made their friends. This was it that ruined them: they <hi type="italic">came against Israel in battle,</hi> and gave the first blow, and therefore <hi type="italic">might have no favour</hi> shown them. Those know not what they do who give the provocation to divine justice, or the authorized instruments of it. <hi type="italic">Are we stronger than God?</hi> Observe here, That hardness of heart is the ruin of sinners. Those that are stupid and secure, and heedless of divine warnings, are already marked for destruction. What hope is there of those concerning whom God has said, <hi type="italic">Go, make their hearts fat?</hi> 2. The constancy of the Israelites in prosecuting this war (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Joshua made war a long time;</hi> some reckon it five years, others seven, that were spent in subduing this land: so long God would train up Israel to war, and give them repeated instances of his power and goodness in every new victory that he gave them. 3. The conquest of the Anakim at last, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.21-Josh.11.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. Either this was done as they met with them where they were dispersed, as some think, or rather it should seem the Anakim had retired to their fastnesses, and so were hunted out and cut off at last, after all the rest of Israel's enemies. The mountains of Judah and Israel were the habitations of those mountains of men; but not their height, nor the strength of their caves, nor the difficulty of the passes to them, could secure, no, not these mighty men, from the sword of Joshua. The cutting off of the sons of Anak is particularly mentioned because these had been such a terror to the spies forty years before, and their bulk and strength had been thought an insuperable difficulty in the way of the reducing of Canaan, <reference osisRef="Num.13.28">Num. xiii. 28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.13.33">33</reference>. Even that opposition which seemed invincible was got over. Never let the sons of Anak be a terror to the Israel of God, for even their day will come to fall. Giants are dwarfs to Omnipotence; yet this struggle with the Anakim was reserved for the latter end of the war, when the Israelites had become more expert in the arts of war, and had had more experience of the power and goodness of God. Note, God sometimes reserves the sharpest trials of his people by affliction and temptation for the latter end of their days. Therefore <hi type="italic">let not him that girds on the harness boast as he that puts it off.</hi> Death, that tremendous son of Anak, is the last enemy that is to be encountered; but it is <hi type="italic">to be destroyed,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.26">1 Cor. xv. 26</reference>. Thanks be to God, who will give us the victory. 4. The end and issue of this long war. The Canaanites were rooted out, not perfectly (as we shall find after in the book of Judges), but in a good measure; they were not able to make any head either, (1.) So as to keep the Israelites out of possession of the land: <hi type="italic">Joshua took all that land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.11.16-Josh.11.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. And we may suppose the people dispersed themselves and their families into the countries they had conquered, at least those that lay nearest to the head-quarters at Gilgal, until an orderly distribution should be made by lot, that every man might know his own. Or, (2.) So as to keep them in action, or give them any molestation (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">The land rested from war.</hi> It ended not in a peace with the Canaanites (that was forbidden), but in a peace from them. There is a rest, a rest from war, remaining for the people of God, into which they shall enter when their warfare is accomplished. <div eID="gen4353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4354" type="x-p"/> II. That which was now done is here compared with that which had been said to Moses. God's word and his works, if viewed and considered together, will mutually illustrate each other. It is here observed in the close, 1. That all the precepts God had given to Moses relating to the conquest of Canaan were obeyed on the people's part, at least while Joshua lived. See how solemnly this is remarked (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">As the Lord commanded Moses his servant,</hi> by whose hand the law was given, <hi type="italic">so did Moses command Joshua,</hi> for Moses was faithful, as a law-giver, to him that appointed him; he did his part, and then he died: but were the commands of Moses observed when he was in his grave? Yes, they were: <hi type="italic">So did Joshua,</hi> who was, in his place, as faithful as Moses in his. <hi type="italic">He left nothing undone</hi> (Heb. he <hi type="italic">removed nothing) of all that the Lord commanded Moses.</hi> Those that leave their duty undone do what they can to remove or make void the command of God, by which they are bound to do it; but Joshua, by performing the precept, <hi type="italic">confirmed</hi> it, as the expression is, <reference osisRef="Deut.27.26">Deut. xxvii. 26</reference>. Joshua was himself a great commander, and yet nothing was more his praise than his obedience. Those that rule others at their will must themselves be ruled by the divine will; then their power is indeed their honour, and not otherwise. The pious obedience for which Joshua is here commended respects especially the command to destroy the Canaanites, and to <hi type="italic">break down their altars and burn their images,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.7.2-Deut.7.5">Deut. vii. 2-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.24">Exod. xxiii. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.13">xxxiv. 13</reference>. Joshua, in his zeal for the Lord of hosts, spared neither the idols nor the idolaters. Saul's disobedience, or rather his partial obedience, to the command of God, for the utter destruction of the Amalekites, cost him his kingdom. It should seem Joshua himself gives this account of his most careful and punctual observance of his orders in the execution of his commission, that in all respects he had done as Moses commanded him; and then it intimates that he had more pleasure and satisfaction in reflecting upon his obedience to the commands of God in all this war, and valued himself more upon that, than upon all the gains and triumphs with which he was enriched and advanced. 2. That all the promises God had given to Moses relating to this conquest were accomplished <hi type="italic">on his part,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.11.23">v. 23</reference>. Joshua <hi type="italic">took the whole land,</hi> conquered it, and took possession of it, <hi type="italic">according to all that the Lord said unto Moses.</hi> God had promised to drive out the nations before them (<reference osisRef="Exod.33.2">Exod. xxxiii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.11">xxxiv. 11</reference>), and to <hi type="italic">bring them down,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.9.3">Deut. ix. 3</reference>. And now it was done. There failed not one word of the promise. Our successes and enjoyments are then doubly sweet and comfortable to us when we see them flowing to us from the promise (this is <hi type="italic">according to what the Lord said</hi>), as our obedience is then acceptable to God when it has an eye to the precept. And, if we make conscience of our duty, we need not question the performance of the promise.  <chapter eID="Josh.11"/> <div eID="gen4354" type="x-p"/>

entries.bbf67e4d42a34eab97713e9603af5c81cc7e16f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2090"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Josh.11.1-Josh.11.9">Jos 11:1-9</reference>. Divers Kings Overcome at the Waters of Merom.</title> <div sID="gen2800" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2090"/><hi type="bold">1-9. And it came to pass, when Jabin king of Hazor had heard those things--</hi>The scene of the sacred narrative is here shifted to the north of Canaan, where a still more extensive confederacy was formed among the ruling powers to oppose the further progress of the Israelites. Jabin ("the Intelligent"), which seems to have been a hereditary title (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.2">Jud 4:2</reference>), took the lead, from Hazor being the capital of the northern region (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.10">Jos 11:10</reference>). It was situated on the borders of lake Merom. The other cities mentioned must have been in the vicinity though their exact position is unknown. <div eID="gen2800" type="x-p"/>
entries.4816e4c409b4f9734e7bce5e8ef032b194b1f68f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2097"/><div sID="gen2813" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2097"/><hi type="bold">11. he burnt Hazor with fire--</hi>calmly and deliberately, doubtless, according to divine direction. <div eID="gen2813" type="x-p"/>
entries.7fb012965215bd6607a6f5b30e32e979b8b98994: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2098"/><div sID="gen2814" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2098"/><hi type="bold">13. as for the cities that stood still in their strength--</hi>literally, "on their heaps." It was a Phoenician custom to build cities on heights, natural or artificial [Hengstenberg]. <div eID="gen2814" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f1ee95fbea0c384634cbf4aeb9c275a9f2dcf22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2099"/><div sID="gen2815" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2099"/><hi type="bold">16. So Joshua took all that land--</hi>Here follows a general view of the conquest. The division of the country there into five parts; namely, the hills, the land of Goshen, that is, a pastoral land near Gibeon (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.41">Jos 10:41</reference>); the valley, the plains and the mountains of Israel, i. e., Carmel, rests upon a diversity of geographical positions, which is characteristic of the region. <div eID="gen2815" type="x-p"/>
entries.723a1095061bff50cfd8689999f88a4957414926: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2100"/><div sID="gen2816" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2100"/><hi type="bold">17. from the mount Halak--</hi>Hebrew, "the smooth mountain."<div eID="gen2816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2817" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that goeth up to Seir--</hi>an irregular line of white naked hills, about eighty feet high, and seven or eight geographical miles in length that cross the whole Ghor, eight miles south of the Dead Sea, probably "the ascent of Akrabbim" [Robinson].<div eID="gen2817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2818" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto Baal-gad in the valley of Lebanon--</hi>the city or temple of the god of destiny, in Baalbec. <div eID="gen2818" type="x-p"/>
entries.9867dafa73f931f9e65e3a29831df83ff5156dac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2101"/><div sID="gen2819" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2101"/><hi type="bold">23. Joshua took the whole land--</hi>The battle of the take of Merom was to the north what the battle of Beth-horon was to the south; more briefly told and less complete in its consequences; but still the decisive conflict by which the whole northern region of Canaan fell into the hands of Israel [Stanley]. <chapter eID="Josh.11"/>

entries.b21e594c8df7cf1bd7a8aaab53e7602717521e21: <div eID="gen7791" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen7792" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7793" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7793" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7792" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7794" type="x-p"/> The Kings of Hazor, Madon, Shimron, and Achshaph, with those of the mountains, plains, etc., and various chiefs of the Canaanites and Amorites, confederate against Israel, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.1-Jos.11.3">Jos 11:1-3</reference>. They pitch their tents at the waters of Merom, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.4">Jos 11:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.5">Jos 11:5</reference>. The Lord encourages Joshua, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.6">Jos 11:6</reference>. He attacks and discomfits them, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.7">Jos 11:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.8">Jos 11:8</reference>. Houghs all their horses, and burns all their chariots, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.9">Jos 11:9</reference>. Takes and burns several of their cities, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.10-Jos.11.13">Jos 11:10-13</reference>. The Israelites take the spoils, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.14">Jos 11:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.15">Jos 11:15</reference>. An account of the country taken by Joshua, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.16-Jos.11.18">Jos 11:16-18</reference>. The Gibeonites only make peace with Israel, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.19">Jos 11:19</reference>. All the rest resist and are overcome, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.20">Jos 11:20</reference>. Joshua cuts off the Anakim, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.21">Jos 11:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.22">Jos 11:22</reference>. The conquered lands are given to Israel, and the war is concluded, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.23">Jos 11:23</reference>. <div eID="gen7794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7795" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen7795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7796" type="x-p"/> Jabin king of Hazor - It is probable that Jabin was the common name of all the kings of Hazor. That king, by whom the Israelites were kept in a state of slavery for twenty years, and who was defeated by Deborah and Barak, was called by this name; see <reference osisRef="Jdg.4.2">Jdg 4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.4.3">Jdg 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.4.23">Jdg 4:23</reference>. The name signifies wise or intelligent. The city of Hazor was situated above the Lake Semechon, in Upper Galilee, according to Josephus, Antiq. lib. v., c. 6. It was given to the tribe of Naphtali, <reference osisRef="Jos.19.36">Jos 19:36</reference>, who it appears did not possess it long; for though it was burnt by Joshua, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.11">Jos 11:11</reference>, it is likely that the Canaanites rebuilt it, and restored the ancient government, as we find a powerful king there about one hundred and thirty years after the death of Joshua, <reference osisRef="Jdg.4.1">Jdg 4:1</reference>. It is the same that was taken by Tiglath-pileser, together with Kadesh, to which it is contiguous; see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Kgs 15:29</reference>. It is supposed to have given name to the Valley or Plain of Hazor or Nasor, situated between it and Kadesh, where Jonathan and Mattathias defeated the armies of Demetrius, and slew three thousand of their men, 1 Maccabees 11:63-74. It was in ancient times the metropolitan city of all that district, and a number of petty kings or chieftains were subject to its king, see <reference osisRef="Jos.11.10">Jos 11:10</reference>; and it is likely that it was those tributary kings who were summoned to attend the king of Hazor on this occasion; for Joshua having conquered the southern part of the promised land, the northern parts seeing themselves exposed made now a common interest, and, joining with Jabin, endeavored to put a stop to the progress of the Israelites. See Calmet <div eID="gen7796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7797" type="x-p"/> Jobab king of Madon - This royal city is nowhere else mentioned in Scripture except in <reference osisRef="Jos.12.19">Jos 12:19</reference>. The Vatican copy of the Septuagint reads Μαρων, Maron, which, if legitimate, Calmet thinks may mean Maronia or Merath in Phoenicia, to the north of Mount Libanus. The Hebrew text reads מרון Meron, <reference osisRef="Jos.12.20">Jos 12:20</reference>, after Shimron, which is probably the same with מדון Madon, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.19">Jos 11:19</reference>, the word having casually dropped out of the preceding place into the latter, and the ר resh and ד daleth being interchanged, which might have easily happened from the great similarity of the letters. Hence Calmet conjectures that it may be the same place with מרוז Meroz, <reference osisRef="Jdg.5.23">Jdg 5:23</reference>, the ז zain and final ן nun being interchanged, which they might easily, as they are so very similar. <div eID="gen7797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7798" type="x-p"/> King of Shimron - This city is supposed to be the same with Symira, in Coelosyria, joined to Maron or Marath, by Pliny and Pomponius Mela. It cannot be Samaria, as that had its name long after by Omri king of Israel. See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.24">1Kgs 16:24</reference>. <div eID="gen7798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7799" type="x-p"/> King of Achshaph - Calmet supposes this to have been the city of Ecdippe, mentioned by Pliny, Ptolemy, Josephus, and Eusebius. The latter places it within ten miles of Ptolemais, on the road to Tyre. It fell to the tribe of Asher. See <reference osisRef="Jos.19.26">Jos 19:26</reference>.
entries.5b06c91be6d80c15a4999aafb36b99f9d7e9b2e7: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen7799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7800" type="x-p"/> On the north of the mountains - Or the mountain, probably Hermon, or some mountain not far from the lake of Gennesareth. <div eID="gen7800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7801" type="x-p"/> And of the plains - That is, the valleys of the above mountains, which had the sea of Chinneroth or Gennesareth on the south. <div eID="gen7801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7802" type="x-p"/> Chinneroth - This city is supposed by St. Jerome and several others since his time, to be the same as was afterwards called Tiberias. From this city or village the sea of Chinneroth or Gennesareth probably had its name. <div eID="gen7802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7803" type="x-p"/> And in the borders of Dor - Calmet supposes this to mean the champaign country of the higher and lower Galilee, on to the Mediterranean Sea, and to the village or city of Dor, which was the farthermost city of Phoenicia. Dor was in the lot of the half tribe of Manasseh, and was situated on the Mediterranean Sea, three leagues from Caesarea, and seven from Ptolemais.
entries.892ce970ac33f3a98729a2e925b0e8b20555d5c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen7803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7804" type="x-p"/> The Canaanite on the east, etc. - Those who dwelt on the borders of Jordan, south of the sea of Tiberias. <div eID="gen7804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7805" type="x-p"/> On the west - Those were the Phoenicians who dwelt on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea, from Dor northwards, on the way to Mount Libanus. - Calmet. <div eID="gen7805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7806" type="x-p"/> The Hivite under Hermon - Mount Hermon was to the east of Libanus and the fountains of Jordan; it is the same with Syrion and Baal Hermon in Scripture. <div eID="gen7806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7807" type="x-p"/> The land of Mizpeh - There were several cities of this name: one in the tribe of Judah, (<reference osisRef="Jos.15.38">Jos 15:38</reference>); a second in the tribe of Benjamin, (<reference osisRef="Jos.18.26">Jos 18:26</reference>); a third beyond Jordan, in the tribe of Gad; and a fourth beyond Jordan, in the tribe of Manasseh, which is that mentioned in the text. See Wells's Geography. Calmet supposes this Mizpeh to be the place where Laban and Jacob made their covenant, and from which circumstance it took its name. See <reference osisRef="Gen.31.48">Gen 31:48</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.49">Gen 31:49</reference>.
entries.2d45376b273207cd9f8a8abaf079df29b7cf02f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen7807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7808" type="x-p"/> Much people, even as the sand - This form of speech, by some called a hyperbole, conveys simply the idea of a vast or unusual number - a number of which no regular estimate could be easily formed. Josephus, who seldom finds difficulties in such cases, and makes no scruple of often speaking without book, tells us that the allied armies amounted to 300,000 foot 10,000 horse, and 20,000 chariots of war. Antiq. lib. v., c. 1. That chariots were frequently used in war, all the records of antiquity prove; but it is generally supposed that among the Canaanites they were armed with iron scythes fastened to their poles and to the naves of their wheels. Terrible things are spoken of these, and the havoc made by them when furiously driven among the ranks of infantry. Of what sort the cavalry was, we know not; but from the account here given we may see what great advantages these allies possessed over the Israelites, whose armies consisted of infantry only.
entries.487f6408a92fed8bcf158c5238003a946ca2d6fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen7808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7809" type="x-p"/> The waters of Merom - Where these waters were, interpreters are not agreed. Whether they were the waters of the Lake Semechon, or the waters of Megiddo, mentioned <reference osisRef="Jdg.5.19">Jdg 5:19</reference>, cannot be easily determined. The latter is the more probable opinion.
entries.70b2725805431a80b4ee3d8b01e46f7eb58e9d1a: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen7809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7810" type="x-p"/> Be not afraid - of them - To meet such a formidable host so well equipped, in their own country, furnished with all that was necessary to supply a numerous army, required more than ordinary encouragement in Joshua's circumstances. This communication from God was highly necessary, in order to prevent the people from desponding on the eve of a conflict, in which their all was at stake.
entries.6b919cd3e8215e89fdb67a411cb79bf2b12a3cf2: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen7810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7811" type="x-p"/> By the waters of Merom suddenly - Joshua, being apprised of this grand confederation, lost no time, but marched to meet them; and before they could have supposed him at hand, fell suddenly upon them, and put them to the rout.
entries.89312628278b693b9bc64586ba92c29c22d5b059: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen7811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7812" type="x-p"/> Great Zidon - If this were the same with the Sidon of the ancients, it was illustrious long before the Trojan war; and both it and its inhabitants are frequently mentioned by Homer as excelling in works of skill and utility, and abounding in wealth: - Ενθ' εσαν οἱ πεπλοι παμποικιλοι, εογα γυναικων Σιδονιων. <div eID="gen7812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7813" type="x-p"/> Iliad, lib. vi., ver. 289. "There lay the ventures of no vulgar art, <div eID="gen7813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7814" type="x-p"/> Sidonian maids embroidered every part." <div eID="gen7814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7815" type="x-p"/> Pope. Αργυρεον κρητηρα τετυγμενον· ἑξ δ' αρα μετρα Χανδανεν, αυταρ καλλει ενικα πασαν επ' αιαν Πολλον, επι Σιδονες πολυδαιδαλοι ευ ησκησαν. <div eID="gen7815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7816" type="x-p"/> Iliad, lib. xxiii., ver. 741. "A silver urn that full six measures held, <div eID="gen7816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7817" type="x-p"/> By none in weight or workmanship excell'd; <div eID="gen7817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7818" type="x-p"/> Sidonian artists taught the frame to shine, <div eID="gen7818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7819" type="x-p"/> Elaborate with artifice divine." <div eID="gen7819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7820" type="x-p"/> Pope. Εκ μεν Σιδωνος πολυχαλκου ευχομαι ειναι. <div eID="gen7820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7821" type="x-p"/> Odyss. xv. 424. "I am of Sidon, famous for her wealth." <div eID="gen7821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7822" type="x-p"/> The art of making glass is attributed by Pliny to this city: Sidon artifex vitri, Hist. Nat. l. v., c. 19. <div eID="gen7822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7823" type="x-p"/> Misrephoth-maim - Or, Misrephoth of the waters. What this place was is unknown, but Calmet conjectures it to be the same with Sarepta, a city of Phoenicia, contiguous to Sidon. The word signifies the burning of the waters, or inflammation; probably it was a place noted for its hot springs: this idea seems to have struck Luther, as he translates it, die warme wasser, the hot waters.
entries.0412670fb6008dee08077b15acc6da55e2d54ce4: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen7823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7824" type="x-p"/> He houghed their horses - The Hebrew word עקר akar, which we render to hough or hamstring, signifies to wound, cut, or lop off. It is very likely that it means here, not only an act by which they were rendered useless, but by which they were destroyed; as God had purposed that his people should not possess any cattle of this kind, that a warlike and enterprising spirit might not be cultivated among them; and that, when obliged to defend themselves and their country, they might be led to depend upon God for protection and victory. On the same ground, God had forbidden the kings of Israel to multiply horses, <reference osisRef="Deu.17.16">Deu 17:16</reference> (note). See the note there containing the reasons on which this prohibition was founded. <div eID="gen7824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7825" type="x-p"/> Burnt their chariots - As these could have been of no use without the horses.
entries.a3dff3b507d9ad0dd8af6757b3724fdb6d80fa78: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen7825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7826" type="x-p"/> Took Hazor - See on <reference osisRef="Jos.11.1">Jos 11:1</reference> (note).
entries.7874d09b1ab63332a3ecc337b71e7b9519f8e20b: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen7826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7827" type="x-p"/> The cities that stood still in their strength - The word תלם tillam, which we translate their strength, and the margin, their heap, has been understood two ways. <div eID="gen7827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7828" type="x-p"/> 1. As signifying those cities which had made peace with the Israelites, when conditions of peace were offered according to the command of the law; and consequently were not destroyed. Such as the cities of the Hivites; see <reference osisRef="Jos.11.19">Jos 11:19</reference>. <div eID="gen7828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7829" type="x-p"/> 2. The cities which were situated upon hills and mountains, which, when taken, might be retained with little difficulty. In this sense the place is understood by the Vulgate, as pointing out the cities quae erant in collibus et tumulis sitae, "which were situated on hills and eminences." As the cities of the plain might be easily attacked and carried, Joshua destroyed them; but as those on mountains, hills, or other eminences, might be retained with little trouble, prudence would dictate their preservation, as places of refuge in any insurrection of the people, or invasion of their adversaries. The passage in Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.18">Jer 30:18</reference>, Jerusalem shall be builded on her own heap, תלה tillah, if understood as above, conveys an easy and clear sense: Jerusalem shall be re-established on her Own Hill.
entries.313cb187f05d9d244ef20453367495bbb100917d: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen7829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7830" type="x-p"/> All the spoil of these cities - Israel took - With the exception of those things which had been employed for idolatrous purposes; see <reference osisRef="Deu.7.25">Deu 7:25</reference>.
entries.0cfe85cd586f1497e43f83ca3ba9202ae9eb288a: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen7830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7831" type="x-p"/> The mountain of Israel, and the valley of the same - This place has given considerable trouble to commentators; and it is not easy to assign such a meaning to the place as may appear in all respects satisfactory. <div eID="gen7831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7832" type="x-p"/> 1. If we consider this verse and the 21st to have been added after the times in which the kingdoms of Israel and Judah were divided, the difficulty is at once removed. <div eID="gen7832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7833" type="x-p"/> 2. The difficulty will be removed if we consider that mountain and valley are put here for mountains and valleys, and that these include all mountains and valleys which were not in the lot that fell to the tribe of Judah. Or, <div eID="gen7833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7834" type="x-p"/> 3. If by mountain of Israel we understand Beth-el, where God appeared to Jacob, afterwards called Israel, and promised him the land of Canaan, a part of the difficulty will be removed. But the first opinion seems best founded; for there is incontestable evidence that several notes have been added to this book since the days of Joshua. See the preface.
entries.a394b827e71d1afcea87a80dfb24a1191df27dcd: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen7834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7835" type="x-p"/> From the mount Halak - All the mountainous country that extends from the south of the land of Canaan towards Seir unto Baal-gad, which lies at the foot of Mount Libanus or Hermon, called by some the mountains of Separation, which serve as a limit between the land of Canaan and that of Seir; see <reference osisRef="Jos.12.7">Jos 12:7</reference>. <div eID="gen7835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7836" type="x-p"/> The valley of Lebanon - The whole extent of the plain which is on the south, and probably north, of Mount Libanus. Calmet conjectures that Coelesyria is here meant.
entries.fc75ecc66a7124002c103a1e8d92fcd6a2a60883: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen7836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7837" type="x-p"/> Joshua made war a long time - The whole of these conquests were not effected in one campaign: they probably required six or seven years. There are some chronological notices in this book, and in Deuteronomy, by which the exact time may be nearly ascertained. Caleb was forty years old when he was sent from Kadesh-barnea by Moses to search out the land, about A.M. 2514; and at the end of this war he was eighty-five years old; (compare <reference osisRef="Jos.14.10">Jos 14:10</reference> with Numbers 13, and Deuteronomy 1); consequently the war ended in 2559, which had begun, by the passage of Jordan, on the tenth day of the first month of the year 2554. From this date to the end of 2559 we find exactly six years; the first of which Joshua seems to have employed in the conquest of the south part of the land of Canaan, and the other five in the conquest of all the territories situated on the north of that country. See Dodd. Calmet computes this differently, and allows the term of seven years for the conquest of the whole land. "Caleb was forty years old when sent from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land. At the conclusion of the war he was eighty-five years old, as himself says, <reference osisRef="Jos.14.10">Jos 14:10</reference>. From this sum of eighty-five subtract forty, his age when he went from Kadesh-barnea, and the thirty-eight years which he spent in the wilderness after his return, and there will remain the sum of seven years, which was the time spent in the conquest of the land." <div eID="gen7837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7838" type="x-p"/> 1. By protracting the war the Canaanites had time to repent, having sufficient opportunity to discern the hand of Jehovah. <div eID="gen7838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7839" type="x-p"/> 2. Agriculture was carried on, and thus provision was made even for the support of the conquerors, for had the land been subdued and wasted at once, tillage must have stopped, and famine would have ensued. <div eID="gen7839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7840" type="x-p"/> 3. Wild beasts would have multiplied upon them, and the land have been desolated by their means. <div eID="gen7840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7841" type="x-p"/> 4. Had these conquests been more rapid the people of Israel would have been less affected, and less instructed by miracles that had passed in such quick succession before their eyes; and, as in this case they would have obtained the dominion with comparatively little exertion, they might have felt themselves less interested in the preservation of an inheritance, to obtain which they had been but at little trouble and little expense. <div eID="gen7841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7842" type="x-p"/> What we labor under the Divine blessing to acquire we are careful to retain; but what comes lightly generally goes lightly. God obliged them to put forth their own strength in this work, and only blessed and prospered them while they were workers together with him. See the note on <reference osisRef="Jos.13.6">Jos 13:6</reference>.
entries.b1a90ccc500fee95df2b61d02a4778a04ff14bf8: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen7842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7843" type="x-p"/> It was of the Lord to harden their hearts - They had sinned against all the light they had received, and God left them justly to the hardness, obstinacy, and pride of their own hearts; for as they chose to retain their idolatry, God was determined that they should be cut off. For as no city made peace with the Israelites but Gibeon and some others of the Hivites, <reference osisRef="Jos.11.19">Jos 11:19</reference>, it became therefore necessary to destroy them; for their refusal to make peace was the proof that they wilfully persisted in their idolatry.
entries.55cd2512c34a4455f004351efeaf1c85f8ee3e19: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen7843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7844" type="x-p"/> Cut off the Anakims - from Hebron, from Debir - This is evidently a recapitulation of the military operations detailed <reference osisRef="Jos.10.36-Jos.10.41">Jos 10:36-41</reference>. <div eID="gen7844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7845" type="x-p"/> Destroyed - their cities - That is, those of the Anakims; for from <reference osisRef="Jos.11.13">Jos 11:13</reference> we learn that Joshua preserved certain other cities.
entries.53c890b81ab09288d723784f55c411b8c453be8a: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen7845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7846" type="x-p"/> In Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod - The whole race of the Anakims was extirpated in this war, except those who had taken refuge in the above cities, which belonged to the Philistines; and in which some of the descendants of Anak were found even in the days of David.
entries.f4383d888211a5c6ece6ce3e3a7cdc0552798b4f: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen7846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7847" type="x-p"/> So Joshua took the whole land - All the country described here and in the preceding chapter. Besides the multitudes that perished in this war, many of the Canaanites took refuge in the confines of the land, and in the neighboring nations. Some suppose that a party of these fugitive Canaanites made themselves masters of Lower Egypt, and founded a dynasty there known by the name of the shepherd kings; but it is more probable that the shepherds occupied Egypt long before the time that Jacob went thither to sojourn. It is said they founded Tingris or Tangier, where, according to Procopius, they erected two white pillars with an inscription in the Phoenician language, of which this is the translation: We Are the Persons Who Have Fled from the Face of Joshua the Plunderer, the Son of Nave or Nun. See Bochart, Phaleg and Canaan, lib. i., c. xxiv., col. 476. Many, no doubt, settled in different parts of Africa, in Asia Minor, in Greece, and in the different islands of the Aegean and Mediterranean Sea: it is supposed also that colonies of this people were spread over different parts of Germany and Sclavonia, etc., but their descendants are now so confounded with the nations of the earth, as no longer to retain their original names, or to be discernible. <div eID="gen7847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7848" type="x-p"/> And Joshua gave it for an inheritance unto Israel - He claimed no peculiar jurisdiction over it; his own family had no peculiar share of it, and himself only the ruined city of Timnath-serah, in the tribe of Ephraim, which he was obliged to rebuild. See <reference osisRef="Jos.19.49">Jos 19:49</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.19.50">Jos 19:50</reference>, and see his character at the end of the book, <reference osisRef="Jos.24.33">Jos 24:33</reference> (note). <div eID="gen7848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7849" type="x-p"/> And the land rested from war - The whole territory being now conquered, which God designed the Israelites should possess at this time. According to the apostle, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.8">Heb 4:8</reference>, etc., Joshua himself was a type of Christ; the promised land, of the kingdom of heaven, the victories which he gained, of the victory and triumph of Christ; and the rest he procured for Israel, of the state of blessedness, at the right hand of God. In this light we should view the whole history, in order to derive those advantages from it which, as a portion of the revelation of God, it was intended to convey. Those who finally reign with Christ are they who, through his grace, conquer the world, the devil, and the flesh; for it is only of those who thus overcome that he says, "They shall sit with me on my throne, as I have overcome, and am set down with the Father on the Father's throne;" <reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Rev 3:21</reference>. Reader, art thou a conqueror?  <chapter eID="Josh.11"/> <div eID="gen7849" type="x-p"/>

entries.815662fef1610fd98ebbfd45b4167d1fc31d054e: The War in Northern Canaan. - <reference osisRef="Josh.11.1">Jos 11:1</reference>-3. On receiving intelligence of what had occurred in the south, the king of Hazor formed an alliance with the kings of Madon, Shimron, and Achshaph, and other kings of the north, to make a common attack upon the Israelites. This league originated with Jabin the king of Hazor, because Hazor was formerly the head of all the kingdoms of northern Canaan (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.10">Jos 11:10</reference>). <hi type="italic">Hazor</hi>, which Joshua conquered and burned to the ground (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.10">Jos 11:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.11">Jos 11:11</reference>), was afterwards restored, and became a capital again (Jdg 4:2; <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.9">1Sa 12:9</reference>); it was fortified by Solomon (1Ki 9:15), and taken by Tiglath-Pileser (2Ki 15:29). It belonged to the tribe of Naphtali (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.36">Jos 19:36</reference>), but has not yet been discovered. According to <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> (Ant. v. 5, 1), it was above the Lake of Samochonitis, the present Bahr el Huleh. <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi> conjectures that it is to be found in the ruins upon Tell <hi type="italic">Khuraibeh</hi>, opposite to the north-west corner of the lake of Huleh, the situation of which would suit Hazor quite well, as it is placed between Ramah and Kedesh in <reference osisRef="Josh.19.35-Josh.19.36">Jos 19:35-36</reference> (see Bibl. Res. p. 364). On the other hand, the present ruins of <hi type="italic">Huzzur</hi> or <hi type="italic">Hazireh</hi>, where there are the remains of large buildings of a very remote antiquity (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Bibl. Res. p. 62), with which <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> identifies Hazor, cannot be thought of for a moment, as these ruins, which are about an hour and a quarter to the south-west of Yathir, are so close to the Ramah of Asher (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.29">Jos 19:29</reference>) that Hazor must also have belonged to Asher, and could not possibly have been included in the territory of Naphtali. There would be more reason for thinking of Tell <hi type="italic">Hazûr</hi> or <hi type="italic">Khirbet Hazûr</hi>, on the south-west of Szafed (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Bibl. Res. p. 81); but these ruins are not very ancient, and only belong to an ordinary village, and not to a town at all. <hi type="italic">Madon</hi> is only mentioned again in <reference osisRef="Josh.12.19">Jos 12:19</reference>, and its situation is quite unknown. <hi type="italic">Shimron</hi>, called Shimron-meron in <reference osisRef="Josh.12.20">Jos 12:20</reference>, was allotted to the tribe of Zebulun (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.15">Jos 19:15</reference>), and is also unknown. For <hi type="italic">Meron</hi> cannot be connected, as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> supposes, with the village and ruins of <hi type="italic">Marôn</hi>, not far from Kedesh, on the south-west (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Pal. iii. p. 371), or <hi type="italic">Shimron</hi> with the ruins of <hi type="italic">Khuraibeh</hi>, an hour to the south of Kedesh; as the territory of Zebulun, to which Shimron belonged, did not reach so far north, and there is not the slightest ground for assuming that there were two Shimrons, or for making a distinction between the royal seat mentioned here and the Shimron of Zebulun. There is also no probability in <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>'s conjecture, that the <hi type="italic">Shimron</hi> last named is the same as the small village of <hi type="italic">Semunieh</hi>, probably the <hi type="italic">Simonias</hi> of <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> (Vita, §24), on the west of Nazareth (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Pal. iii. p. 201). <hi type="italic">Achshaph</hi>, a border town of Ashwer (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.25">Jos 19:25</reference>), is also unknown, and is neither to be sought, as <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi> supposes (Bibl. Res. pp. 55), in the ruins of Kesâf, which lie even farther north than <hi type="italic">Abel</hi> (<hi type="italic">Abil</hi>), in the tribe of Naphtali, and therefore much too far to the north to have formed the boundary of Asher; nor to be identified with Acco (<hi type="italic">Ptolemais</hi>), as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> imagines, since Acco has nothing in common with <hi type="italic">Achshaph</hi> except the letter <hi type="italic">caph</hi> (see also at <reference osisRef="Josh.19.25">Jos 19:25</reference>).
entries.2d655ec582f50f0ff8f28a879d26d9c4cea4c4cc: <reference osisRef="Josh.11.2">Jos 11:2</reference> <div eID="gen2814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2815" type="x-p"/> Jabin also allied himself with the kings of the north “<hi type="italic">upon the mountains</hi>,” i.e., the mountains of Naphtali (<reference osisRef="Josh.20.7">Jos 20:7</reference>), and “<hi type="italic">in the Arabah to the south of Chinnereth</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.35">Jos 19:35</reference>), i.e., in the Ghor to the south of the sea of Galilee, and “<hi type="italic">in the lowland</hi>,” i.e., the northern portion of it, as far down as Joppa, and “<hi type="italic">upon the heights of Dor</hi>.” The town of <hi type="italic">Dor</hi>, which was built by Phoenicians, who settled there on account of the abundance of the purple mussels (<hi type="italic">Steph. Byz. s. v.</hi> Δῶρος), was allotted to the Manassites in the territory of Asher (<reference osisRef="Josh.17.11">Jos 17:11</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.19.26">Jos 19:26</reference>), and taken possession of by the children of Joseph (<reference osisRef="1Chr.7.29">1Ch 7:29</reference>). It was situated on the Mediterranean Sea, below the promontory of Carmel, nine Roman miles north of Caesarea, and is at the present time a hamlet called <hi type="italic">Tantura</hi> or <hi type="italic">Tortura</hi>, with very considerable ruins (<hi type="italic">Wilson</hi>, The Holy Land, ii. 249, and <hi type="italic">V. de Velde</hi>, Journey, i. p. 251). The old town was a little more than a mile to the north, on a small range of hills, which is covered with ruins (<hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, Erdk. xvi. pp. 608-9; <hi type="italic">V. de Velde</hi>, Mem. p. 307), and on the north of which there are rocky ranges, with many grottos, and houses cut in the rock itself (<hi type="italic">Buckingham</hi>, Syria, i. pp. 101-2). These are “the heights of Dor,” or “the high range of Dor” (<reference osisRef="Josh.12.23">Jos 12:23</reference>; 1Ki 4:11).
entries.3fde33b7d858ad54365062bf969fafcfc8471273: <reference osisRef="Josh.11.3">Jos 11:3</reference> <div eID="gen2815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2816" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Namely, with the Canaanites on the east and west, the Amorites</hi>” and other tribes dwelling upon the mountains (vid., <reference osisRef="Josh.3.10">Jos 3:10</reference>), and “<hi type="italic">the Hivites under the Hermon in the land of Mizpah</hi>,” i.e., the country below <hi type="italic">Hasbeya</hi>, between <hi type="italic">Nahr Hasbany</hi> on the east, and <hi type="italic">Merj. Ayûn</hi> on the west, with the village of <hi type="italic">Mutulleh</hi> or <hi type="italic">Mtelleh</hi>, at present inhabited by Druses, which stands upon a hill more than 200 feet high, and from which there is a splendid prospect over the Huleh basin. It is from this that it has derived its name, which signifies prospect, <hi type="italic">specula</hi>, answering to the Hebrew <hi type="italic">Mizpah</hi> (see <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi>, Bibl. Res. p. 372).
entries.d051a22cbca722986dd5ed0c6b303add9c2928ab: <reference osisRef="Josh.11.4-Josh.11.5">Jos 11:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen2816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2817" type="x-p"/> These came out with their armies, a people as numerous as the sand by the sea-shore (vid., <reference osisRef="Gen.22.17">Gen 22:17</reference>, etc.), and very many horses and chariots. All these kings agreed together, sc., concerning the war and the place of battle, and encamped at Merom to fight against Israel. The name <hi type="italic">Merom</hi> (<hi type="italic">Meirûm</hi> in the Arabic version) answers to <hi type="italic">Meirôm</hi>, a village whose name is also pronounced <hi type="italic">Meirûm</hi>, a celebrated place of pilgrimage among the Jews, because Hillel, Shammai, Simeon ben Jochai, and other noted Rabbins are said to be buried there (see <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi>, Pal. iii. p. 333), about two hours’ journey north-west of Szafed, upon a rocky mountain, at the foot of which there is a spring that forms a small brook and flows away through the valley below Szafed (<hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, R. ii. pp. 127-8; <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi>, Bibl. Res. pp. 73ff.). This stream, which is said to reach the Lake of Tiberias, in the neighbourhood of Bethsaida, is in all probability to be regarded as the “waters of Merom,” as, according to <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> (Ant. v. 1, 18), “these kings encamped at Berothe (de. Bell. Jud. xx. 6, and Vit. 37, '<hi type="italic">Meroth</hi>'), a city of Upper Galilee, not far from Kedese.”<note placement="foot">The traditional opinion that “waters of Merom” is the Old Testament name for the Lake of Samochonitis, or Huleh, is not founded upon any historical evidence, but is simply an inference of <hi type="italic">Hadr. Reland</hi> (Pal. Ill. p. 262), (1) from the statement made by <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> (Ant. v. 5, 1), that Hazor was above the Lake of Somochonitis, it being taken for granted without further reason that the battle occurred at Hazor, and (2) from the supposed similarity in the meaning of the names, viz., that <hi type="italic">Samochonitis</hi> is derived from an Arabic word signifying to be high, and therefore means the same as <hi type="italic">Merom</hi> (height), though here again the <hi type="italic">zere</hi> is disregarded, and <hi type="italic">Merom</hi> is arbitrarily identified with <hi type="italic">Marom</hi>.</note>
entries.d78e699ef88273c489efbdf2f071d81f6de288f6: <reference osisRef="Josh.11.6">Jos 11:6</reference> <div eID="gen2817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2818" type="x-p"/> On account of this enormous number, and the might of the enemy, who were all the more to be dreaded because of their horses and chariots, the Lord encouraged Joshua again,<note placement="foot">“As there was so much more difficulty connected with the destruction of so populous and well-disciplined an army, it was all the more necessary that he should be inspired with fresh confidence. For this reason God appeared to Joshua, and promised him the same success as He had given him so many times before.” - <hi type="italic">Calvin</hi>.</note> as in <reference osisRef="Josh.8.1">Jos 8:1</reference>, by promising him that on the morrow He would deliver them all up slain before Israel; only Joshua was to lame their horses (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.6">Gen 49:6</reference>) and burn their chariots. אנכי before נתן gives emphasis to the sentence: “I will provide for this; by my power, which is immeasurable, as I have shown thee so many times, and by my nod, by which heaven and earth are shaken, shall these things be done” (<hi type="italic">Masius</hi>).
entries.72905e0401a050dcaf36366a818b77c769497553: <reference osisRef="Josh.11.7-Josh.11.8">Jos 11:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen2818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2819" type="x-p"/> With this to inspirit them, the Israelites fell upon the enemy and smote them, chasing them towards the north-west to Sidon, and westwards as far as Misrephothmaim, and into the plain of Mizpah on the east. <hi type="italic">Sidon</hi> is called the great (as in <reference osisRef="Josh.19.28">Jos 19:28</reference>), because at that time it was the metropolis of Phoenicia; whereas even by the time of David it had lost its ancient splendour, and was outstripped by its daughter city Tyre. It is still to be seen in the town of <hi type="italic">Saida</hi>, a town of five or six thousand inhabitants, with many large and well-built houses (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Pal. iii. p. 415, and <hi type="italic">Movers</hi>, Phönizier, ii. 1, pp. 86ff.). <hi type="italic">Misrephothmaim</hi> (mentioned also at <reference osisRef="Josh.13.6">Jos 13:6</reference>), which the Greek translators have taken as a proper name, though the Rabbins and some Christian commentators render it in different ways, such as salt-pits, smelting-huts, or glass-huts (see <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> Thes. p. 1341), is a collection of springs, called <hi type="italic">Ain Mesherfi</hi>, at the foot of the promontory to which with its steep pass the name of <hi type="italic">Ras el Nakhûra</hi> is given, the <hi type="italic">scala Tyriorum</hi> or <hi type="italic">Passepoulain</hi> of the Crusaders (see <hi type="italic">V. de Velde</hi>, Mem. p. 335, and <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, Erdk. xvi. p. 807). מצפּה בּקעת (Eng. Ver. “the valley of Mizpeh”) is probably the basin of the <hi type="italic">Huleh</hi> lake and of <hi type="italic">Nahr Hasbany</hi>, on the western side of which lay the land of <hi type="italic">Mizpah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.3">Jos 11:3</reference>).
entries.f77b841dff83fe7a17a5e74914c9fcb12222f655: <reference osisRef="Josh.11.9">Jos 11:9</reference> <div eID="gen2819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2820" type="x-p"/> Joshua carried out the command of the Lord with regard to the chariots and horses.
entries.bb774e03cd1a22037af433a60d78ccd8a7d7d278: <reference osisRef="Josh.11.10-Josh.11.15">Jos 11:10-15</reference> <div eID="gen2820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2821" type="x-p"/> After destroying the foe, and returning from the pursuit, Joshua took Hazor, smote its king and all the inhabitants with the edge of the sword, and burned the town, the former leader of all those kingdoms. He did just the same to the other towns, except that he did not burn them, but left them standing upon their hills. על־תּלּם העמחות (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.13">Jos 11:13</reference>) neither contains an allusion to any special fortification of the towns, nor implies a contrast to the towns built in the valleys and plains, but simply expresses the thought that these towns were still standing upon their hill, i.e., upon the old site (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.30.18">Jer 30:18</reference> : the participle does not express the preterite, but the present). At the same time, the expression certainly implies that the towns were generally built upon hills. The pointing in תּלּם is not to be altered, as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> suggests. The singular “<hi type="italic">upon their hill</hi>” is to be taken as distributive: standing, now as then, each upon its hill. - With <reference osisRef="Josh.11.15">Jos 11:15</reference>, “<hi type="italic">as Jehovah commanded His servant Moses</hi>” (cf. Num 33:52.; Deu 7:1., <reference osisRef="Deut.20.16">Deu 20:16</reference>), the account of the wars of Joshua is brought to a close, and the way opened for proceeding to the concluding remarks with reference to the conquest of the whole land (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.16-Josh.11.23">Jos 11:16-23</reference>). דּבר הסיר לא, he put not away a word, i.e., left nothing undone.
entries.30067188351665c120239eb53e0b7b473fd6cd10: <reference osisRef="Josh.11.16-Josh.11.17">Jos 11:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen2821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2822" type="x-p"/> Retrospective View of the Conquest of the Whole Land. - <reference osisRef="Josh.11.16">Jos 11:16</reference>, Jos 11:17. Joshua took all this land, namely, those portions of Southern Canaan that have already been mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.10.40-Josh.10.41">Jos 10:40-41</reference>; also the Arabah, and the mountains of Israel and its lowlands (see <reference osisRef="Josh.11.2">Jos 11:2</reference>), i.e., the northern part of the land (in the campaign described in <reference osisRef="Josh.11.1-Josh.11.15">Jos 11:1-15</reference>), that is to say, Canaan in all its extent, “<hi type="italic">from the bald mountain which goeth up to Seir</hi>” in the south, “<hi type="italic">to Baal-gad, in the valley of Lebanon under Hermon</hi>.” The “<hi type="italic">bald mountain</hi>” (<hi type="italic">Halak</hi>), which is mentioned here and in <reference osisRef="Josh.12.7">Jos 12:7</reference> as the southern boundary of Canaan, is hardly the row of white cliffs which stretches obliquely across the Arabah eight miles below the Dead Sea and forms the dividing line that separates this valley into <hi type="italic">el-Ghor</hi> and <hi type="italic">el-Araba</hi> (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Pal. ii. pp. 489, 492), or the present <hi type="italic">Madara</hi>, a strange-looking chalk-hill to the south-west of the pass of Sufah (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> ii. p. 589), a steep bare mountain in a barren plain, the sides of which consist of stone and earth of a leaden ashy hue (<hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, R. iii. pp. 14, 15); but in all probability the northern edge of the Azazimeh mountain with its white and glistening masses of chalk. <hi type="italic">Baal-gad</hi>, i.e., the place or town of Baal, who was there worshipped as Gad (see <reference osisRef="Isa.65.11">Isa 65:11</reference>), also called <hi type="italic">Baal-hermon</hi> in Jdg 3:3 and <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.23">1Ch 5:23</reference>, is not Baalbek, but the <hi type="italic">Paneas</hi> or <hi type="italic">Caesarea Philippi</hi> of a later time, the present <hi type="italic">Banjas</hi> (see at Num 34:8-9). This is the opinion of <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi> and <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi>, though <hi type="italic">Van de Velde</hi> is more disposed to look for Baal-gad in the ruins of <hi type="italic">Kalath</hi> (the castle of) <hi type="italic">Bostra</hi>, or of <hi type="italic">Kalath Aisafa</hi>, the former an hour and a half, the latter three hours to the north of Banjas, the situation of which would accord with the biblical statements respecting Baal-gad exceedingly well. The “<hi type="italic">valley of Lebanon</hi>” is not <hi type="italic">Coele-Syria</hi>, the modern <hi type="italic">Bekâa</hi>, between Lebanon and Antilibanus, but the valley at the foot of the southern slope of Jebel Sheik (Hermon).
entries.16c0f17e65c6944840c3c8c294268b2f2cb09d54: <reference osisRef="Josh.11.18-Josh.11.20">Jos 11:18-20</reference> <div eID="gen2822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2823" type="x-p"/> Joshua made war with the kings of Canaan a long time; judging from <reference osisRef="Josh.14.7">Jos 14:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.14.10">Jos 14:10</reference>, as much as seven years, though <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> (Ant. v. 1, 19) speaks of five (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.14.10">Jos 14:10</reference>). No town submitted peaceably to the Israelites, with the exception of Gibeon: they took the whole in war. “<hi type="italic">For it was of the Lord</hi>” (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.20">Jos 11:20</reference>), i.e., God ordered it so that they (the Canaanites) hardened their heart to make war upon Israel, that they might fall under the ban, and be destroyed without mercy. On the hardening of the heart as a work of God, see the remarks upon the hardening of Pharaoh (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.21">Exo 4:21</reference>). It cannot be inferred from this, that if the Canaanites had received the Israelites amicably, God would have withdrawn His command to destroy them, and allowed the Israelites to make peace with them; for when they made peace with the Gibeonites, they did not inquire what as the will of the Lord, but acted in opposition to it (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.9.14">Jos 9:14</reference>). The remark is made with special reference to this, and has been correctly explained by <hi type="italic">Augustine</hi> (qu. 8 in Jos.) as follows: “Because the Israelites had shown mercy to some of them of their own accord, though in opposition to the command of God, therefore it is stated that they (the Canaanites) made war upon them so that none of them were spared, and the Israelites were not induced to show mercy to the neglect of the commandment of God.”
entries.e9c0ddb9f1bcc52afc4a97db8e7cab59bab92590: <reference osisRef="Josh.11.21-Josh.11.23">Jos 11:21-23</reference> <div eID="gen2823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2824" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Josh.11.21">Jos 11:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.22">Jos 11:22</reference>, the destruction of the Anakites upon the mountains of Judah and Israel is introduced in a supplementary form, which completes the history of the subjugation and extermination of the Canaanites in the south of the land (Josh 10). This supplement is not to be regarded either as a fragment interpolated by a different hand, or as a passage borrowed from another source. On the contrary, the author himself thought it necessary, having special regard to Num 13:28, Num 13:31., to mention expressly that Joshua also rooted out from their settlements the sons of Anak, whom the spies in the time of Moses had described as terrible giants, and drove them into the Philistine cities of Gaza, Bath, and Ashdod. “<hi type="italic">At that time</hi>” points back to the “long time,” mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.11.18">Jos 11:18</reference>, during which Joshua was making war upon the Canaanites. The words “cut off,” etc., are explained correctly by <hi type="italic">Clericus</hi>: “Those who fell into his hands he slew, the rest he put to flight, though, as we learn from <reference osisRef="Josh.15.14">Jos 15:14</reference>, they afterwards returned.” (On the <hi type="italic">Anakim</hi>, see at Num 13:22.) They had their principal settlement upon the mountains in Hebron (<hi type="italic">el Khulil</hi>, see <reference osisRef="Josh.10.3">Jos 10:3</reference>), Debir (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.10.38">Jos 10:38</reference>), and Anab. The last place (<hi type="italic">Anab</hi>), upon the mountains of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.50">Jos 15:50</reference>), has been preserved along with the old name in the village of <hi type="italic">Anâb</hi>, four or five hours to the south of Hebron, on the eastern side of the great Wady <hi type="italic">el Khulil</hi>, which runs from Hebron down to Beersheba (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Pal. ii. p. 193). “<hi type="italic">And from all</hi> (the rest of) <hi type="italic">the mountains of Judah, and all the mountains of Israel</hi>:” the latter are called the mountains of Ephraim in Jos 17:15. The two together form the real basis of the land of Canaan, and are separated from one another by the large Wady <hi type="italic">Beit Hanina</hi> (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Pal. ii. p. 333). They received their respective names from the fact that the southern portion of the mountain land of Canaan fell to the tribe of Judah as its inheritance, and the northern part to the tribe of Ephraim and other tribes of Israel.<note placement="foot">The distinction here made may be explained without difficulty even from the circumstances of Joshua’s own time. Judah and the double tribe of Joseph (Ephraim and Manasseh) received their inheritance by lot before any of the others. But whilst the tribe of Judah proceeded into the territory allotted to them in the south, all the other tribes still remained in Gilgal; and even at a later period, when Ephraim and Manasseh were in their possessions, all Israel, with the exception of Judah, were still encamped at Shiloh.
